x-a: Investment Advisory & Financial Planning Basics
In a structured financial planning engagement, which step must come before recommending any specific investment product?
Executing transactions through the client's broker
Reviewing the performance of the recommended portfolio
Understanding the client's goals, financial position and risk profile
Fixing the adviser's renewal fee for the next year
Recommendations can only be suitable once the adviser has gathered data on the client's goals, finances and risk profile; implementation and monitoring come later.
Investment Advisory & Financial Planning Basics
Riya, 28, has three goals: a house down payment in 3 years, retirement at 58, and her newborn's higher education in 18 years. Which goal should normally be funded with the least volatile assets?
The house down payment in 3 years
Retirement at 58
The child's higher education in 18 years
All three goals equally, regardless of horizon
The shortest-horizon goal has the least time to recover from a market fall, so it should be matched with stable, low-volatility assets.
Investment Advisory & Financial Planning Basics
A client in the early-career accumulation stage of the financial life cycle typically has:
A need to convert most assets into regular income immediately
A long investment horizon and a relatively high capacity to take investment risk
A short horizon and a focus on preserving capital
Mainly estate-transfer and succession concerns
Young earners have decades of future income ahead, which gives them a long horizon and greater ability to absorb short-term volatility.
Time Value of Money
A client invests ₹1,00,000 for 5 years at 8% per annum compounded annually. What will the investment be worth at maturity (approximately)?
Time Value of Money
A client needs ₹10,00,000 in 10 years. If money can earn 7% per annum compounded annually, how much must be invested today as a lump sum (approximately)?
Time Value of Money
A loan carries a nominal rate of 12% per annum compounded monthly. What is its effective annual rate (approximately)?
EAR = (1 + 0.12/12)^12 − 1 = (1.01)^12 − 1 ≈ 12.68%. 12.36% would be the result of half-yearly compounding.
Time Value of Money
An investor starts a SIP of ₹10,000 at the end of every month for 10 years in a fund assumed to earn 12% per annum compounded monthly. What is the approximate value at the end of 10 years?
₹12.0 lakh
₹21.0 lakh
₹27.4 lakh
₹23.0 lakh
FV of an ordinary annuity = 10,000 × [(1.01)^120 − 1] ÷ 0.01 ≈ 10,000 × 230.04 ≈ ₹23.0 lakh, against total contributions of ₹12 lakh.
Client Financial Position & Debt Management

A client owns a house worth ₹60 lakh, mutual funds of ₹15 lakh, bank balances of ₹5 lakh and a car worth ₹5 lakh. He owes ₹25 lakh on a home loan, ₹3 lakh on a car loan and ₹50,000 on a credit card. What is his net worth?
₹85 lakh
₹57 lakh
₹56.5 lakh
₹51.5 lakh
Total assets = 60 + 15 + 5 + 5 = ₹85 lakh; total liabilities = 25 + 3 + 0.5 = ₹28.5 lakh; net worth = 85 − 28.5 = ₹56.5 lakh.
Client Financial Position & Debt Management
A client's gross monthly income is ₹1,20,000 and she pays EMIs of ₹30,000 on a home loan and ₹6,000 on a car loan. What is her debt-service (EMI-to-income) ratio?
Debt-service ratio = total EMIs ÷ gross income = (30,000 + 6,000) ÷ 1,20,000 = 30%.
Client Financial Position & Debt Management
A client has a revolving credit-card balance charging about 36% a year and holds a fixed deposit earning 7%, over and above a separate emergency fund. What is the most sensible advice?
Keep paying the minimum due and retain the FD
Invest the FD in equity funds to try to out-earn the card interest
Take a personal loan to buy more FDs
Use the fixed deposit to clear the credit-card balance
Repaying a 36% debt is a guaranteed 'return' far higher than the 7% FD, and the emergency fund is already provided for separately.
Indian Financial Markets
Which of the following is a money market instrument?
A 10-year Government of India dated security
An equity share of a listed company
A 91-day Treasury bill
A 15-year infrastructure bond
Money market instruments have original maturities of up to one year; a 91-day T-bill qualifies, whereas the others are long-term capital market instruments.
Indian Financial Markets
Which regulator primarily governs the call money market in India?
Securities and Exchange Board of India
Reserve Bank of India
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority
The call money market is an interbank money market and falls under the RBI's regulatory domain.
Securities Market Segments
When a company sells newly issued shares to the public for the first time through an IPO, the transaction takes place in the:
Primary market
Secondary market
Over-the-counter derivatives market
Money market
Fresh issuance of securities by the issuer to investors is a primary market activity; later trading between investors happens in the secondary market.
Securities Market Segments
What is the standard (rolling) settlement cycle for trades in the equity cash segment of Indian stock exchanges?
India completed its move to T+1 settlement for the equity cash segment in 2023; an optional same-day cycle exists only for a limited set of stocks.
Equity Investment
A share trades at ₹450 and the company's earnings per share for the latest year is ₹30. What is its price-to-earnings ratio?
6.7 times
13.5 times
30 times
15 times
P/E = market price ÷ EPS = 450 ÷ 30 = 15 times.
Equity Investment
A company pays an annual dividend of ₹12 per share and its share trades at ₹400. What is the dividend yield?
Dividend yield = dividend per share ÷ market price = 12 ÷ 400 = 3%.
Equity Investment
What is the usual effect of a 1:1 bonus issue on an existing shareholder?
The shareholder receives cash equal to the face value of the shares held
The company's net worth doubles
The shareholder's ownership percentage doubles
The number of shares doubles and the market price adjusts to roughly half, leaving total value broadly unchanged
A bonus issue capitalises reserves into share capital; shares outstanding double but nothing of value enters the company, so the price adjusts and each holder's percentage stake is unchanged.
Equity Investment
Under SEBI's market-capitalisation categorisation used by mutual funds, a 'large-cap' company is one that is:
Ranked 1st to 100th by full market capitalisation
Ranked 1st to 250th by full market capitalisation
Any company with a market capitalisation above ₹5,000 crore
Ranked 101st to 250th by full market capitalisation
SEBI defines large caps as the top 100 companies by full market cap, mid caps as 101st–250th and small caps as 251st onwards.
Debt Investment
If market interest rates rise, what happens to the price of an existing fixed-coupon bond?
It rises
It stays at face value until maturity
It rises only if the coupon is above the new market rate
It falls
Bond prices move inversely to yields: new bonds now offer higher coupons, so existing bonds must trade at lower prices to offer a competitive yield.
Debt Investment
A bond with face value ₹100 pays an annual coupon of 8% and currently trades at ₹95. What is its current yield?
Current yield = annual coupon ÷ market price = 8 ÷ 95 ≈ 8.42%.
Debt Investment
A bond has a Macaulay duration of 6 years and a YTM of 9% (annual compounding). If its yield rises by 50 basis points, what is the approximate change in its price?
A fall of about 3.00%
A fall of about 2.75%
A rise of about 2.75%
A fall of about 5.50%
Modified duration = 6 ÷ 1.09 ≈ 5.50; price change ≈ −5.50 × 0.5% ≈ −2.75%.
Debt Investment
Which risk is eliminated for an investor who buys a zero-coupon bond and holds it to maturity?
Reinvestment risk
Default risk
Inflation risk
Liquidity risk if the investor needs money early
A zero-coupon bond pays no interim coupons, so there are no cash flows to reinvest; the investor still bears credit and inflation risk.
Derivatives
An investor buys a call option with a strike price of ₹500 by paying a premium of ₹20. At expiry the underlying settles at ₹540. What is the net profit per share (ignoring costs)?
Payoff = 540 − 500 = ₹40; net profit = 40 − 20 premium = ₹20 per share.
Derivatives
Which statement correctly distinguishes the buyer of an option from the buyer of a futures contract?
Both have only a right and no obligation
The futures buyer pays a non-refundable premium
The option buyer has a right but no obligation, while the futures buyer is obliged to settle the contract
The option buyer must deposit margin and settle mark-to-market losses daily
An option buyer pays a premium for the right to exercise; a futures contract binds both parties, which is why futures positions carry margins and daily mark-to-market.
Derivatives
An investor with a diversified equity portfolio wants protection against a sharp market fall but wishes to keep the benefit of any rise. Which strategy fits best?
Selling index call options
Buying index put options
Buying index futures
Buying index call options
A long put gains when the index falls, offsetting portfolio losses, while the upside is retained less the premium paid; selling calls caps the upside and offers little downside protection.
Mutual Funds
A scheme holds investments worth ₹120 crore, has accrued expenses and other liabilities of ₹2 crore and has 8 crore units outstanding. What is its NAV per unit?
NAV = (assets − liabilities) ÷ units = (120 − 2) ÷ 8 = ₹14.75.
Mutual Funds
For income-tax purposes, a mutual fund scheme is treated as 'equity-oriented' when it invests at least what proportion of its corpus in equity shares of domestic listed companies?
The tax definition of an equity-oriented fund requires a minimum 65% investment in domestically listed equity shares.
Mutual Funds
A client wants to park surplus cash for about two months with very low risk and easy access. Which mutual fund category is most suitable?
Small-cap fund
Gilt fund with 10-year constant duration
Sectoral equity fund
Liquid fund
Liquid funds invest in money market instruments of up to 91 days' maturity, giving low volatility and quick redemption suitable for very short horizons.
Mutual Funds
Compared with the regular plan of the same mutual fund scheme, the direct plan:
Has a lower expense ratio because no distributor commission is built in
Has a different portfolio managed by another fund manager
Charges a higher exit load
Is available only to investors routed through a distributor
Direct and regular plans share the same portfolio; the direct plan excludes distribution commission, so its expense ratio is lower and its NAV grows faster.
Real Estate, Gold & Other Assets
SEBI's REIT regulations require a REIT to distribute what minimum share of its net distributable cash flows to unitholders?
REITs must distribute at least 90% of net distributable cash flows, which is why they are viewed as income-oriented investments.
Real Estate, Gold & Other Assets
A client wants exposure to gold purely as an investment. Compared with buying jewellery, the key advantage of a gold ETF is that it:
Avoids making charges and purity concerns, and is held in demat form
Guarantees a fixed annual interest over and above the gold price
Is completely free of gold-price risk
Is exempt from all taxes on sale

Gold ETF units are backed by high-purity physical gold held by a custodian, traded on exchanges and held in demat, avoiding jewellery's making charges and purity risk; they still carry gold-price risk.
PMS, AIF & Other Managed Portfolios
What is the minimum investment SEBI requires from a client of a portfolio management service (PMS)?
₹10 lakh
₹50 lakh
₹25 lakh
₹1 crore
SEBI's Portfolio Managers Regulations set the minimum investment per client at ₹50 lakh (in cash or securities).
PMS, AIF & Other Managed Portfolios
Under SEBI's AIF Regulations, what is the general minimum investment by an investor (other than an accredited investor or eligible employees/directors) in an Alternative Investment Fund?
₹10 lakh
₹50 lakh
₹1 crore
₹5 crore
AIFs generally require a minimum commitment of ₹1 crore per investor, with lower thresholds only for specified employees/directors and relaxation for accredited investors.
PMS, AIF & Other Managed Portfolios
Which statement best describes a discretionary portfolio management service?
The client must approve every trade before execution
The portfolio manager takes buy and sell decisions for the client's account without seeking approval for each transaction
The manager only gives advice and the client executes trades
The portfolio is pooled with other clients and units are issued
In discretionary PMS the client delegates investment decisions to the manager within the agreed mandate; in non-discretionary PMS each decision needs client consent.
Asset Allocation & Portfolio Construction
Which statement best distinguishes tactical from strategic asset allocation?
Tactical allocation is the client's permanent long-term policy mix
Tactical allocation makes short-term deviations from the long-term policy mix to exploit market views
Strategic allocation changes every week based on market news
The two terms mean the same thing
Strategic allocation is the long-term mix based on goals and risk profile; tactical allocation temporarily tilts away from it based on market outlook.
Asset Allocation & Portfolio Construction
Diversification reduces portfolio risk the most when the returns of the assets combined have:
Perfect positive correlation (+1)
High positive correlation (around +0.8)
Identical standard deviations
Low or negative correlation with each other
When returns do not move together, losses in one asset tend to be offset by others; at +1 correlation there is no diversification benefit.
Asset Allocation & Portfolio Construction
A portfolio is 60% in equity expected to return 12%, 30% in debt expected to return 7% and 10% in gold expected to return 9%. What is the expected portfolio return?
Asset Allocation & Portfolio Construction
A client's agreed allocation is 60% equity and 40% debt. After a strong equity rally the portfolio stands at 72% equity and 28% debt. What does disciplined rebalancing require?
Buy more equity to ride the momentum
Do nothing, since the portfolio has made gains
Sell part of the equity and add to debt to restore 60:40
Move the entire portfolio into debt
Rebalancing brings the portfolio back to the policy mix, which here means trimming the overweight equity and adding to the underweight debt.
Portfolio Performance Evaluation
A fund returned 14% with a standard deviation of 16%. The risk-free rate is 6%. What is its Sharpe ratio?
Sharpe ratio = (14 − 6) ÷ 16 = 0.50.
Portfolio Performance Evaluation
A fund earned 13% with a beta of 1.4 when the risk-free rate was 6%. What is its Treynor ratio?
Treynor ratio = (13 − 6) ÷ 1.4 = 5.0 (percentage points of excess return per unit of beta).
Portfolio Performance Evaluation
A fund with beta 1.2 earned 15% in a year when the market returned 12% and the risk-free rate was 6%. What is its Jensen's alpha?
CAPM expected return = 6 + 1.2 × (12 − 6) = 13.2%; alpha = 15 − 13.2 = 1.8%.
Behavioural Finance
An investor quickly sells shares that have gained but keeps holding shares that have fallen, hoping they will recover. This pattern is known as:
Home bias
Disposition effect
Herd behaviour
Mental accounting of windfall gains
The disposition effect, rooted in loss aversion, is the tendency to realise gains too early and hold on to losers too long.
Behavioural Finance
After one year of very high equity returns, a client insists on raising his equity allocation sharply because he expects the same returns to continue. Which bias is he most likely showing?
Anchoring to purchase price
Loss aversion
Status quo bias
Recency bias
Recency bias is giving excessive weight to recent events and extrapolating them into the future.
Operational Aspects (KYC, Demat, Transactions)
What is the main purpose of a KYC Registration Agency (KRA) in the Indian securities market?
To hold KYC records centrally so that KYC done with one intermediary can be used by other intermediaries
To approve the investment advice given to clients
To settle trades between buyers and sellers
To act as a depository for dematerialised shares
KRAs centralise KYC records, so investors need not repeat full KYC with every SEBI-registered intermediary.
Operational Aspects (KYC, Demat, Transactions)
Which are the two depositories that hold dematerialised securities in India?
NSE and BSE
NSDL and CDSL
CAMS and KFintech
NSCCL and ICCL
NSDL and CDSL are the depositories; NSE/BSE are exchanges, CAMS/KFintech are registrars and NSCCL/ICCL are clearing corporations.
Regulatory Framework for Investment Advisers
Under the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, from whom may a registered investment adviser receive remuneration for advice given to a client?
Only from the client
From the asset management companies whose schemes are recommended
From both the client and product manufacturers, if disclosed
From the stock exchange through which trades are executed
SEBI's framework requires IAs to be paid only by clients, so that advice is not influenced by commissions from product providers.
Regulatory Framework for Investment Advisers
Before recommending an investment, a SEBI-registered investment adviser must ensure that the advice is:
Approved in advance by the client's bank
Suitable for the client, based on a documented risk profile
Limited to products listed on a stock exchange
Identical to the advice given to all other clients
The IA Regulations require risk profiling and a suitability assessment so that recommendations match each client's risk capacity, objectives and circumstances.
Regulatory Framework for Investment Advisers
Which of the following is exempt from registering as an investment adviser under the SEBI (IA) Regulations?
A person charging clients a fee to recommend specific stocks
An IRDAI-registered insurance agent advising solely on insurance products
A firm selling paid stock-tip subscriptions through a messaging app
An individual offering fee-based mutual fund portfolio advice to the public
The regulations exempt, among others, insurance agents and brokers giving advice only on insurance products; anyone charging for securities advice must register.
Ethics, Conflicts & Grievance Redressal
An investor is not satisfied with the response of a SEBI-registered investment adviser to his complaint. Where can he escalate it online?
IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal
The RBI Integrated Ombudsman
The PFRDA grievance system
SEBI's SCORES platform
SCORES is SEBI's online grievance redressal system for complaints against SEBI-registered intermediaries; unresolved disputes can then go to online dispute resolution.
Ethics, Conflicts & Grievance Redressal
An investment adviser is about to recommend a scheme whose fund manager is her spouse. What is the appropriate course of action?
Disclose the relationship to the client before giving advice and recommend the scheme only if it is suitable
Recommend the scheme without mention, since the adviser earns no commission
Refuse to advise the client on any mutual funds
Ask the fund manager to approve the recommendation
Ethical and regulatory norms require material conflicts of interest to be disclosed, and the advice must still rest on suitability for the client.
x-b: Risk Management & Insurance Concepts
For a risk that has low probability but very high potential financial loss, such as premature death of the main earner, the most appropriate risk-management technique is usually:
Risk retention by paying losses from savings
Risk transfer through insurance
Ignoring the risk because it is unlikely
Risk reduction by cutting household expenses
Low-frequency, high-severity risks cannot be absorbed by most households, so they are best transferred to an insurer.
Risk Management & Insurance Concepts
While buying a life policy, Kunal did not disclose that he was being treated for diabetes. Which insurance principle has he breached?
Indemnity
Subrogation
Contribution
Utmost good faith
Insurance contracts require utmost good faith, under which the proposer must disclose all material facts; non-disclosure can lead to the claim being repudiated.
Risk Management & Insurance Concepts
Why does the principle of indemnity generally not apply to life insurance?
Because life insurance is not a contract
Because the value of a human life cannot be precisely measured, so a fixed sum assured is paid
Because life insurance claims are always paid in instalments
Because life insurance does not require insurable interest
Indemnity restores the insured to the pre-loss position, which works for measurable property losses; life insurance is a benefit policy paying a pre-agreed sum.
Risk Management & Insurance Concepts
Ravi wants to buy life insurance policies on several people. In which case does he lack insurable interest?
On the life of his neighbour
On his own life
On the life of his wife
On the life of a borrower, to the extent of the loan he has given
Insurable interest requires a financial loss on the insured person's death; a person has it in himself, his spouse and a debtor to the extent of the debt, but not in an unrelated neighbour.
Life Insurance Products
Which feature correctly describes a pure term life insurance plan?
It pays the sum assured plus bonuses on survival to maturity
It invests premiums in market-linked funds chosen by the policyholder
It provides cover for the whole of life and builds a high surrender value
It gives the largest cover per rupee of premium and pays only on death during the term
A term plan has no savings component, so premiums are low relative to the sum assured and the benefit is payable only on death within the policy term.
Life Insurance Products
What is the lock-in period applicable to a unit-linked insurance plan (ULIP)?
5 years
3 years
7 years
10 years
IRDAI rules impose a five-year lock-in on ULIPs, during which money cannot be withdrawn even if the policy is discontinued.
Life Insurance Products
A policyholder stops paying premiums on a traditional endowment policy after it has acquired a surrender value and does not surrender it. What generally happens?
The policy lapses with no benefit at all
The insurer refunds all premiums with interest
The policy continues as a paid-up policy with a reduced sum assured
The full original sum assured stays in force without further premiums
Once a traditional policy acquires surrender value, non-payment converts it into a paid-up policy whose sum assured is reduced in proportion to premiums paid.
Life Insurance Products
A businessman is worried that, after his death, his creditors may claim the proceeds of his life policy meant for his wife and children. What is the most suitable solution?
Name his business partner as nominee
Take a policy under Section 6 of the Married Women's Property Act in favour of his wife and children
Assign the policy to his main lender
Buy a ULIP instead of a term plan
A policy under the MWP Act creates a trust for the wife and children, so its proceeds are outside the reach of the insured's creditors and estate.
Life Insurance Products
Anil, 29, is the sole earner for his wife and young child and has a limited budget. He wants adequate protection for his family. What is the most suitable recommendation?
A small endowment policy with a sum assured equal to one year's income
A single-premium ULIP using all his savings
A term plan with a large sum assured, investing the premium saved separately
No life cover until his income increases
With dependants and limited money, a term plan provides the high cover needed at the lowest cost, leaving room to invest separately for goals.
Health & General Insurance
In a family floater health policy, the sum insured:
Is separately available in full to each covered member
Applies only to the eldest member
Is shared by all covered family members and can be used by any one or more of them
Is paid only on the death of a member
A floater pools one sum insured across the family; one member's large claim can exhaust it for others in that policy year.
Health & General Insurance
A health policy has a 20% co-payment clause. A policyholder makes an admissible hospitalisation claim of ₹2,00,000 within the sum insured. How much will the insurer pay?
With a 20% co-payment, the insured bears 20% (₹40,000) and the insurer pays 80% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹1,60,000.
Health & General Insurance
How does a super top-up health policy differ from a regular top-up policy?
A super top-up has no deductible at all
A regular top-up covers only critical illnesses
A super top-up applies its deductible to the total of claims in a policy year, not to each claim separately
A super top-up can be bought only by senior citizens
A regular top-up pays only when a single claim exceeds the deductible; a super top-up pays once aggregate claims in the year cross the deductible.
Health & General Insurance
Which motor insurance cover is compulsory for vehicles plying in public places in India?
Own-damage cover
Zero-depreciation add-on
Third-party liability insurance
Engine-protection add-on
The Motor Vehicles Act mandates third-party liability cover; own-damage cover and add-ons are optional.
Insurance Needs Analysis
Sanjay contributes ₹9 lakh a year to his family's needs and has 20 working years left. Using a 6% discount rate and assuming year-end contributions, what is his human life value (approximately)?
₹1.03 crore
₹1.80 crore
₹0.90 crore
₹1.25 crore
Insurance Needs Analysis

Using the need-based approach: a client's outstanding home loan is ₹40 lakh, children's education needs ₹30 lakh (present value), family living-expense corpus needs ₹1.2 crore, existing investments are ₹50 lakh and existing life cover is ₹25 lakh. What additional life cover is required?
₹1.15 crore
₹1.90 crore
₹1.40 crore
₹1.65 crore
Total need = 40 + 30 + 120 = ₹190 lakh; less resources of 50 + 25 = ₹75 lakh; additional cover = ₹115 lakh = ₹1.15 crore.
Insurance Needs Analysis
How does the human life value (HLV) approach essentially estimate life insurance need?
By capitalising the future income the insured would have contributed to the family
By adding up only the outstanding loans of the insured
By multiplying current premium by the policy term
By taking the market value of the insured's house
HLV treats a person as an income-generating asset and values the present value of future contributions to dependants.
Insurance Needs Analysis
Meera, 35, relies only on her employer's group health cover for herself and her family. What is the most appropriate advice?
No action is needed because group cover continues for life
Cancel the group cover and rely on savings
Buy an independent family health policy, since group cover may end with the job and fresh cover later may face waiting periods
Buy additional life insurance in place of health insurance
Group cover is linked to employment; an individual policy taken early builds continuity and gets past waiting periods while she is young and healthy.
Retirement Planning Concepts
In retirement planning, 'longevity risk' refers to the risk that:
Interest rates rise just before retirement
The retiree outlives the retirement corpus
The retiree dies before retirement
Equity markets fall in the first year of retirement
Longevity risk is the danger of living longer than planned, so that savings run out while the retiree still needs income.
Retirement Planning Concepts
A couple's current living expenses are ₹50,000 a month. With 6% annual inflation, what monthly amount will they need to maintain the same lifestyle in 25 years (approximately)?
₹2.15 lakh
₹1.25 lakh
₹1.60 lakh
₹3.05 lakh
Retirement Planning Concepts
Two retirees have the same average return over 20 years, but one suffers large losses in the first two years of withdrawals and runs out of money earlier. This illustrates:
Reinvestment risk
Currency risk
Liquidity premium
Sequence-of-returns risk
When withdrawals are being made, poor returns early in retirement deplete the corpus faster, even if the long-run average is unchanged.
Retirement Planning Concepts
The 'income replacement ratio' in retirement planning means:
The proportion of salary saved every month
The ratio of pension to provident fund balance
The percentage of pre-retirement income needed to maintain the desired lifestyle after retirement
The share of equity in a retirement portfolio
The replacement ratio expresses post-retirement income needs as a percentage of pre-retirement income and is a quick way to size retirement needs.
Retirement Products & Pension Schemes
What is the basic tenure of a Public Provident Fund (PPF) account and the maximum deposit allowed in a financial year?
15 years; ₹1.5 lakh
10 years; ₹2 lakh
15 years; ₹2.5 lakh
21 years; ₹1.5 lakh
A PPF account matures after 15 years (extendable in blocks of five years) and accepts up to ₹1.5 lakh per financial year.
Retirement Products & Pension Schemes
Under the Employees' Provident Fund scheme, the standard employee contribution is:
8.33% of gross salary
12% of basic wages plus dearness allowance
10% of gross salary including all allowances
A fixed ₹1,800 per month
Employees contribute 12% of basic wages plus DA; the employer's matching contribution is split between EPF and the Employees' Pension Scheme.
Retirement Products & Pension Schemes
Which statement about NPS Tier II accounts is correct?
It is the mandatory pension account with withdrawal restrictions
It can be opened without a Tier I account
Withdrawals from it must be used to buy an annuity
It is a voluntary savings account with flexible withdrawals that requires an active Tier I account
Tier I is the core pension account with exit rules; Tier II is an optional, withdrawable add-on available only to Tier I holders.
Retirement Products & Pension Schemes
Which person is eligible to join Atal Pension Yojana?
A 45-year-old self-employed person
A 25-year-old who pays income tax
A 60-year-old retired government employee
A 30-year-old savings account holder who is not an income-tax payer
APY is open to citizens aged 18–40 with a bank or post office savings account; since October 2022, income-tax payers cannot join.
Retirement Products & Pension Schemes
What is the maximum amount an individual can invest in the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme and its basic tenure?
₹15 lakh; 5 years
₹30 lakh; 10 years
₹30 lakh; 5 years
₹50 lakh; 3 years
SCSS allows an aggregate investment of up to ₹30 lakh per individual for a five-year tenure, extendable by three years.
Retirement Corpus & Distribution Planning

A client will need ₹6 lakh a year in today's terms after retirement for 25 years, withdrawn at the beginning of each year. If the corpus earns a real (inflation-adjusted) return of 2%, what corpus is needed at retirement in today's terms (approximately)?
₹1.50 crore
₹1.19 crore
₹1.06 crore
₹0.98 crore
Retirement Corpus & Distribution Planning
A client wants to accumulate ₹1 crore in 20 years by investing an equal amount at the end of each year in a portfolio expected to earn 10% a year. What annual investment is required (approximately)?
₹1.75 lakh
₹5.00 lakh
₹1.17 lakh
₹2.35 lakh
Retirement Corpus & Distribution Planning
A retiring couple wants guaranteed income for life for both of them and also wants the capital to pass to their children after both have died. Which annuity option fits best?
Single life annuity without return of purchase price
Annuity certain for 5 years
Joint life, last survivor annuity with return of purchase price
Single life annuity with return of purchase price on the husband's life only
A joint-life last-survivor annuity continues until the second death, and the return-of-purchase-price feature pays the capital to nominees afterwards.
Retirement Corpus & Distribution Planning
In the 'bucket strategy' for managing a retirement corpus, the near-term bucket is typically invested in:
Small-cap equity funds for maximum growth
Liquid and low-risk instruments to meet the next few years' expenses
Real estate that can be sold when needed
Long-dated zero-coupon bonds
The bucket approach keeps near-term spending money safe and liquid, while longer-term buckets hold growth assets that have time to recover from volatility.
Income Tax Fundamentals
How does residential status affect the scope of an individual's taxable income in India?
Both residents and non-residents are taxed only on salary income
A resident is generally taxed on global income, while a non-resident is taxed only on income received, accruing or arising in India
Non-residents are taxed on global income and residents only on Indian income
Residential status matters only for companies
Residential status determines scope: residents are taxed on worldwide income, whereas non-residents are taxed only on India-sourced or India-received income.
Income Tax Fundamentals
Under which head of income is interest earned on a savings bank account taxed?
Income from other sources
Capital gains
Profits and gains of business or profession
Income from house property
Interest on bank deposits is not covered by any specific head, so it is taxed as income from other sources.
Income Tax Fundamentals
For individual taxpayers, which tax regime currently applies by default unless the taxpayer opts out?
The old regime with all deductions
Whichever regime the employer chooses
A flat-rate regime for all incomes
The new (concessional-rate) tax regime
Since FY 2023-24 the new regime is the default for individuals; they must actively opt for the old regime to claim most deductions.
Income Tax Fundamentals
Rajesh gifts ₹10 lakh to his wife, who invests it in a fixed deposit. In whose hands is the interest on that deposit generally taxed?
His wife's, since the deposit is in her name
Rajesh's, under the clubbing provisions
Split equally between them
Nobody's, since gifts to a spouse are exempt
Income from assets transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration is clubbed with the income of the transferor.
Taxation of Investment Products
How are capital gains taxed on a pure debt mutual fund (investing almost entirely in bonds and money market instruments) bought after 1 April 2023?
At a concessional long-term rate after 36 months with indexation
Fully exempt if held for more than 3 years
At a flat 10% without indexation
At the investor's applicable slab rate, regardless of holding period
Since 1 April 2023, gains on such debt funds are deemed short-term and taxed at slab rates whatever the holding period.
Taxation of Investment Products

An investor sells listed equity shares held for 3 years and makes a long-term capital gain of ₹3,25,000 in the year (STT paid, no other gains). Under the rules applicable to transfers after 23 July 2024, what is the tax before surcharge and cess?
LTCG above ₹1.25 lakh on listed equity is taxed at 12.5%: (3,25,000 − 1,25,000) × 12.5% = ₹25,000.
Taxation of Investment Products
How are dividends received from Indian companies and mutual funds taxed for a resident individual?
Added to income and taxed at the investor's slab rate
Fully exempt in the investor's hands
Taxed only through distribution tax paid by the company
Taxed at a flat 12.5% as capital gains
Since FY 2020-21, dividend income is taxable in the shareholder's hands at applicable slab rates.
Taxation of Investment Products
For capital-gains purposes, listed equity shares become long-term assets when held for:
More than 24 months
More than 36 months
More than 6 months
More than 12 months
Listed securities (and equity-oriented fund units) qualify as long-term when held for more than 12 months.
Wealth Management & Estate Planning Concepts
What is the primary objective of estate planning?
Maximising short-term portfolio returns
Orderly transfer of a person's assets to intended beneficiaries with minimum disputes, delay and cost
Avoiding all taxes legally payable during one's lifetime
Increasing the person's borrowing capacity
Estate planning arranges how wealth passes on death or incapacity so that beneficiaries receive it smoothly as intended.
Wealth Management & Estate Planning Concepts
Mohan nominated his elder son for his bank deposit but his valid will leaves the deposit to his daughter. After his death, what is the position?
The son becomes the absolute owner because nomination overrides a will
The deposit is forfeited to the government
The bank pays the son as nominee, but he holds the money in trust for the daughter, who is entitled under the will
The bank must split the deposit equally among all children
A nominee gives the institution a valid discharge but is a custodian for those entitled under succession law or the will.
Wealth Management & Estate Planning Concepts
A general power of attorney given by an individual automatically ceases:
After exactly one year
On the death of the person who granted it
When the agent changes address
Only when a court cancels it
An agent's authority under a power of attorney ends on the principal's death; thereafter the estate is dealt with under the will or succession law.
Wills, Succession & Trusts
Which of the following is required for a will to be validly executed in India (other than a privileged will)?
Compulsory registration with the sub-registrar
Execution on stamp paper of a specified value
Signature of the testator, attested by at least two witnesses
Approval by all legal heirs
An unprivileged will must be signed by the testator and attested by two or more witnesses; registration and stamp paper are not mandatory.
Wills, Succession & Trusts
Under Muslim personal law, up to what portion of his estate can a Muslim generally bequeath by will without the consent of his heirs?
One-half
One-third
Two-thirds
The entire estate
A Muslim can bequeath up to one-third of the net estate by will; bequests beyond that need the heirs' consent.
Wills, Succession & Trusts
What is a probate?
A document by which a person gives up rights in property
A registration certificate for a trust
An affidavit filed by the nominee of a bank account
A copy of a will certified under the seal of a competent court, granting administration of the estate to the executor
Probate establishes the validity of a will and confirms the executor's authority to administer the estate.
Wills, Succession & Trusts
A Hindu man dies without a will, leaving his wife, his mother, his father, one son and one daughter. Under the Hindu Succession Act, how is his self-acquired property shared?
Each of the five takes one-fifth
The son takes half and the rest share the balance
Wife takes half; the son and daughter share the other half
Wife, mother, son and daughter take one-fourth each; the father takes nothing
Wife, mother, son and daughter are Class I heirs and share equally; the father is a Class II heir and inherits only if there is no Class I heir.
Wills, Succession & Trusts
In a private trust, the person who creates the trust and transfers property to it is called the:
Settlor
Trustee
Beneficiary
Executor
The settlor (author) creates the trust; the trustee holds and manages the property for the beneficiaries.
Comprehensive Financial Planning & Case Studies

Amit, 40, earns ₹24 lakh a year, his wife is a homemaker and they have two school-going children. He has a ₹50 lakh home loan, ₹20 lakh in mutual funds and a ₹50 lakh term cover. What is the most pressing gap in his plan?
He holds too little gold
He should prepay the home loan using all mutual funds
He should stop investing for retirement
His life cover is inadequate relative to his liabilities and family's future needs
As the sole earner with a large loan and dependants, a ₹50 lakh cover barely matches the loan; protection must be fixed before growth goals.
Comprehensive Financial Planning & Case Studies
When a client has limited surplus, which should normally be addressed first in a financial plan?
Buying a second home for investment
Building an emergency fund and adequate insurance cover
Investing in a sector fund for high returns
Planning for a foreign holiday
Protection and liquidity form the foundation of a plan; without them, an emergency can derail all other goals.
Comprehensive Financial Planning & Case Studies
A child's higher education costs ₹20 lakh today. If education inflation is 8% a year, what will it cost in 12 years (approximately)?
₹39.2 lakh
₹43.0 lakh
₹62.8 lakh
₹50.4 lakh
Comprehensive Financial Planning & Case Studies
Which event should most clearly trigger a review of a client's financial plan outside the regular review cycle?
The birth of a child
A one-day fall of 1% in the market index
A change in the colour of the fund factsheet
A routine monthly SIP debit
Major life events change goals, cash flows and protection needs, so the plan should be revisited when they occur.
xv: Introduction to Research Analyst Profession
How does a buy-side analyst differ from a sell-side analyst?
A buy-side analyst only recommends buying, never selling
A buy-side analyst researches for the internal use of an investing institution such as an AMC, while a sell-side analyst's research is distributed to clients of a broker
A sell-side analyst works only for insurance companies
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
Buy-side research supports the analyst's own institution's investment decisions; sell-side research is published for brokerage clients.
Introduction to Research Analyst Profession
Which activity is the core function of a research analyst?
Executing client orders on the stock exchange
Holding client securities in safe custody
Analysing securities and issuing research reports with recommendations or opinions
Underwriting public issues
Research analysts analyse issuers and securities and publish reports, recommendations or price targets; execution, custody and underwriting are other intermediaries' roles.
Introduction to Research Analyst Profession
An analyst at an integrated firm is asked by the investment banking team to upgrade a stock because the company is a prospective banking client. What should the analyst do?
Upgrade the stock to support the banking relationship
Maintain an independent view and not let the banking team influence the rating
Ask the company's management to choose the rating
Delay the report until the deal closes and then upgrade
Research must be independent and objective; firms are required to keep research insulated from investment banking pressure.
Introduction to Securities Market
What role does a clearing corporation play in exchange-traded markets?
It acts as the central counterparty, guaranteeing settlement of trades
It lists companies and approves IPO prices
It issues credit ratings for debt securities
It decides the dividends paid by listed companies
By becoming buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer, the clearing corporation removes counterparty risk from exchange trades.
Introduction to Securities Market
What is the main function of a depository in the Indian securities market?
Fixing the market price of shares
Holding securities in electronic (dematerialised) form and recording their transfer
Lending money to investors for margin trading
Approving corporate actions of listed companies
Depositories such as NSDL and CDSL maintain electronic holdings and effect transfers through depository participants.
Introduction to Securities Market
Indices such as the Nifty 50 are weighted by free-float market capitalisation. Free float generally excludes:
Shares held by retail investors
Shares held by foreign portfolio investors
Shares held by promoters and promoter groups
Shares held by mutual funds
Free float counts only shares readily available for trading, so promoter and similar locked-in holdings are excluded.
Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets
A company splits each share of face value ₹10 into shares of face value ₹2. An investor holding 100 shares will now hold:
100 shares, with the face value unchanged
200 shares, with the price halving
500 shares, with the market price adjusting to about one-fifth
500 shares, with the price unchanged
Splitting ₹10 into ₹2 creates five shares for each one held; the total value is unchanged, so the price falls to about one-fifth.
Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets
A company has equity share capital of ₹50 crore and reserves of ₹250 crore, with 10 crore shares outstanding. What is its book value per share?
Book value per share = (50 + 250) ÷ 10 = ₹30.
Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets
Yield to maturity (YTM) of a bond represents:
The return earned if the bond is held to maturity and all coupons are reinvested at the same yield
The coupon divided by face value
The annual coupon divided by current price only
The return earned if the bond is sold the next day
YTM is the discount rate that equates the bond's price to its future cash flows, implicitly assuming holding to maturity and reinvestment at the YTM.
Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets
A debt instrument rated 'D' by an Indian credit rating agency signifies that it:
Has the highest degree of safety
Is a deposit product of a bank
Is a short-term instrument of high safety
Is in default or expected to be in default
'D' is the lowest rating, indicating default; 'AAA' indicates the highest safety for long-term instruments.
Fundamentals of Research
Which statement correctly contrasts fundamental and technical analysis?
Technical analysis relies on balance sheets, while fundamental analysis uses only charts
Both rely only on management interviews
Fundamental analysis estimates intrinsic value from economic, industry and company factors, while technical analysis studies price and volume patterns
Fundamental analysis is used only for bonds
Fundamental analysts ask what a security is worth; technical analysts study market data to judge likely price movement.
Fundamentals of Research
In the top-down approach to equity research, the analyst begins with:
Selection of individual companies, then the industry
Technical charts of the chosen stock
The company's dividend history only
Analysis of the economy, then the industry, and finally the company
Top-down research moves from macro conditions to attractive sectors and then to companies within them; bottom-up starts with the company.
Fundamentals of Research
Which of the following is primary data for an analyst researching a consumer company?
The company's published annual report
Industry statistics released by a trade association
Information gathered from the analyst's own checks with distributors and retailers
A government survey of household consumption
Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher; published reports and statistics are secondary data.
Fundamentals of Research
In technical analysis, a 'golden cross' occurs when:
The price falls below its 200-day moving average
Trading volume falls to a yearly low
A shorter-term moving average (e.g. 50-day) crosses above a longer-term moving average (e.g. 200-day)
A stock hits its upper circuit limit
A golden cross is generally read as a bullish signal; the reverse crossover is called a death cross.
Economic Analysis

In an economy, private consumption is ₹150 lakh crore, investment ₹50 lakh crore, government spending ₹40 lakh crore, exports ₹30 lakh crore and imports ₹35 lakh crore. What is GDP by the expenditure method?
₹305 lakh crore
₹235 lakh crore
₹270 lakh crore
₹240 lakh crore
Economic Analysis
If the RBI raises the policy repo rate, which effect is most likely in the short run?
Bank lending rates fall, boosting loan demand
Bond prices rise sharply across maturities
Borrowing costs rise, which tends to weigh on rate-sensitive sectors such as real estate and autos
Inflation immediately rises due to cheaper credit
A repo hike tightens liquidity and raises borrowing costs, hurting interest-sensitive demand and typically lowering bond prices.
Economic Analysis
Which inflation measure does the RBI's flexible inflation-targeting framework use?
Wholesale Price Index
GDP deflator
Index of Industrial Production
Consumer Price Index (Combined)
The framework targets CPI-Combined headline inflation, with a target of 4% and a tolerance band of ±2 percentage points.
Economic Analysis
The fiscal deficit of the government is best defined as:
Revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts
Imports minus exports
Total borrowings minus interest payments
Total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings
Fiscal deficit measures the government's total borrowing requirement: expenditure in excess of non-debt receipts.
Economic Analysis
Nominal GDP grew 11% in a year and the GDP deflator rose 4%. What is the real GDP growth rate (exact)?
Real growth = (1.11 ÷ 1.04) − 1 ≈ 6.73%; simple subtraction gives about 7% only as an approximation.
Industry Analysis
Which of the following is NOT one of Porter's five competitive forces?
The central bank's monetary policy stance
Threat of new entrants
Bargaining power of buyers
Threat of substitute products
Porter's five forces are rivalry, threat of entrants, threat of substitutes and the bargaining power of buyers and suppliers; monetary policy is a macro factor.
Industry Analysis
An industry is showing slowing sales growth, stable cash flows, intense competition for market share and consolidation. It is most likely in which stage of its life cycle?
Maturity
Pioneering
Rapid growth
Start-up
Mature industries grow roughly in line with the economy, generate steady cash and often consolidate as players fight for share.
Industry Analysis
Which sector is generally considered defensive, with relatively stable demand across economic cycles?
Cement
Automobiles
Capital goods
Fast-moving consumer goods
Demand for daily essentials holds up in downturns, whereas cement, autos and capital goods are cyclical.
Industry Analysis
In an industry, three firms hold 85% market share and building a new plant takes about four years and large capital. What does this imply?
Perfect competition with no pricing power
High entry barriers and an oligopolistic structure that may give incumbents pricing power
Very low barriers to entry
That the industry must be in the pioneering stage
Concentrated share plus long, capital-heavy gestation deters entrants, supporting incumbents' pricing power.
Company Analysis – Business & Governance
Which is the best example of an economic moat?
A one-time gain from sale of land
A payments platform that becomes more valuable to each user as more users join
A temporary spike in commodity prices
A large cash balance raised through a recent IPO
Network effects create a durable competitive advantage that rivals find hard to replicate; one-offs are not moats.
Company Analysis – Business & Governance
Which combination is a corporate governance red flag for an analyst?
A board with a majority of independent directors
Consistent dividend payouts and timely disclosures
Long tenure of a reputed statutory auditor without qualifications
Rising pledging of promoter shares together with large related-party transactions
Heavy promoter pledging signals financial stress and large related-party dealings can divert value from minority shareholders.
Company Analysis – Business & Governance
In a SWOT analysis of a pharmaceutical company, a new government order capping the price of its main product is classified as a:
Strength
Weakness
Opportunity
Threat
Threats are external developments that can hurt the business; price controls are imposed from outside the company.
Company Analysis – Business & Governance
Under SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements, related-party transactions of a listed company require prior approval of:
The statutory auditor
The audit committee
The stock exchange
The company's largest customer
LODR requires all related-party transactions to be approved in advance by the audit committee, with material ones also needing shareholder approval.
Company Analysis – Financial Analysis
A company has current assets of ₹300 crore and current liabilities of ₹200 crore. What is its current ratio?
Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities = 300 ÷ 200 = 1.5.
Company Analysis – Financial Analysis
A company has total debt of ₹400 crore and shareholders' equity of ₹800 crore. What is its debt-to-equity ratio?
Debt-to-equity = 400 ÷ 800 = 0.5.
Company Analysis – Financial Analysis
A company has a net profit margin of 8%, asset turnover of 1.5 times and an equity multiplier (assets/equity) of 2. Using DuPont analysis, what is its ROE?
Company Analysis – Financial Analysis
A company's EBIT is ₹120 crore and its interest expense is ₹30 crore. What is its interest coverage ratio?
3 times
4 times
0.25 times
5 times
Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ interest = 120 ÷ 30 = 4 times.
Company Analysis – Financial Analysis
A company reports steadily rising net profits, but its cash flow from operations has been negative for three years as receivables balloon. What should an analyst infer?
The company is in excellent financial health
Negative operating cash flow always signals heavy expansion capex
Cash flows are irrelevant when profits are rising
Earnings quality is questionable and revenue recognition or working capital needs scrutiny
Profits not converting into cash, especially with rising receivables, can indicate aggressive accounting or weak collections.
Company Analysis – Financial Analysis
A company has inventory of ₹72 crore and annual cost of goods sold of ₹438 crore. Using a 365-day year, what are its inventory days?
60 days
72 days
30 days
6 days
Inventory days = inventory ÷ COGS × 365 = 72 ÷ 438 × 365 = 60 days.
Corporate Valuation

A company has just paid a dividend of ₹10 per share. Dividends are expected to grow at 6% a year forever and the required return is 12%. What is the share's intrinsic value under the Gordon growth model?
D1 = 10 × 1.06 = 10.6; value = 10.6 ÷ (0.12 − 0.06) = ₹176.67. Using D0 instead of D1 would wrongly give ₹166.67.
Corporate Valuation
A firm has EBIT of ₹200 crore, a tax rate of 25%, depreciation of ₹40 crore, capital expenditure of ₹60 crore and an increase in working capital of ₹20 crore. What is its free cash flow to the firm?
₹110 crore
₹150 crore
₹130 crore
₹160 crore
FCFF = EBIT(1 − t) + D&A − capex − ΔWC = 150 + 40 − 60 − 20 = ₹110 crore.
Corporate Valuation
A company has market capitalisation of ₹1,000 crore, debt of ₹300 crore, cash of ₹100 crore and EBITDA of ₹150 crore. What is its EV/EBITDA multiple?
8.0 times
6.7 times
9.3 times
8.7 times
Corporate Valuation
An analyst forecasts next year's EPS at ₹45 and believes the stock deserves a forward P/E of 20 times. What is the implied target price?
Target price = forward EPS × target P/E = 45 × 20 = ₹900.
Corporate Valuation
A firm is financed 60% by equity costing 14% and 40% by debt with a pre-tax cost of 10%. The tax rate is 25%. What is its WACC?
Corporate Valuation
When computing terminal value in a DCF with the perpetual growth method, the terminal growth rate must be:
Lower than the discount rate and sustainable over the long run
Higher than the discount rate
Equal to the current year's revenue growth
Equal to the discount rate
TV = FCF(n+1) ÷ (WACC − g) is meaningful only if g is below WACC; a perpetual rate above long-run economic growth is not sustainable.
Fundamentals of Risk and Return
The risk-free rate is 7%, a stock's beta is 1.3 and the expected market return is 13%. What is the stock's required return under CAPM?
Fundamentals of Risk and Return
Which type of risk can be largely eliminated by holding a well-diversified portfolio?
Systematic (market) risk
Interest-rate risk affecting all securities
Risk arising from a nationwide recession
Unsystematic (company-specific) risk
Company-specific shocks offset each other in a diversified portfolio; market-wide risk remains.
Fundamentals of Risk and Return
An investor buys a share at ₹200, receives a dividend of ₹6 during the year and sells it at ₹230. What is the holding-period return?
Fundamentals of Risk and Return
A stock has a beta of 0.7. What does this indicate?
It will always return 70% of the market return
It has 70% probability of rising
Its returns have tended to move about 0.7% for every 1% move in the market
It has no systematic risk
Beta measures sensitivity to market movements; below 1 means the stock has historically been less volatile than the market.
Qualities of a Good Research Report
Which element is essential in a good equity research report?
Guaranteed returns over the target horizon
Key risks that could invalidate the investment thesis
The analyst's personal portfolio returns
Only positive information about the company
A balanced report states its assumptions and the risks that could make the recommendation wrong, so readers can judge it.
Qualities of a Good Research Report
A good research report's recommendation should ideally specify:
Only the current market price
Only the company's logo and history
The rating, the target price and the time horizon, with the valuation basis
A list of stocks the analyst dislikes
A clear rating with target price, horizon and valuation method makes the recommendation actionable and verifiable.
Qualities of a Good Research Report
An analyst hears an unverified market rumour that a company under coverage is about to be acquired. What is the appropriate response?
Include it as the main reason for a buy rating
Not present it in the report as fact, and verify it only through legitimate public sources
Trade on it personally before publishing
Ask a friend at the company for confidential details
Reports must rest on verified information; seeking or using unpublished price-sensitive information would breach insider trading rules.
Legal and Regulatory Environment

Under SEBI's Research Analyst Regulations, a research analyst and its associates are prohibited from trading in a security they recommend during which period around the publication of a research report?
5 days before and 30 days after publication
7 days before and 7 days after publication
30 days before and 5 days after publication
Only on the day of publication
The regulations bar dealing in the recommended security or its derivatives from 30 days before to 5 days after the report is published.
Legal and Regulatory Environment

A research analyst must disclose in the report if it or its associates hold actual or beneficial ownership of at least what percentage of the subject company's securities, measured at the end of the month before publication?
Holdings of 1% or more in the subject company must be disclosed as a potential conflict of interest.
Legal and Regulatory Environment
During a management meeting, an analyst learns of unannounced quarterly results that will move the share price. Under SEBI's insider trading regulations, the analyst:
May trade freely because he is not an employee of the company
May publish it immediately in a report to clients
Must not trade in the securities or pass the information on until it is generally available
May share it with his firm's trading desk
Unpublished price-sensitive information makes the analyst an insider; trading on it or communicating it is prohibited.
Legal and Regulatory Environment
For what minimum period must a research analyst maintain records such as research reports and the basis of recommendations under SEBI's regulations?
5 years
1 year
3 years
10 years
The RA Regulations require records to be maintained for at least five years.
xvii: Retirement Planning: An Overview
Which trend has most increased the importance of individual retirement planning in India?
Rising life expectancy combined with the shift towards nuclear families
Falling life expectancy
Universal defined-benefit pensions for all private employees
A steady decline in healthcare costs
People live longer and can rely less on joint-family support, so they must fund longer retirements themselves.
Retirement Planning: An Overview
The National Pension System is an example of which type of pension arrangement?
Defined benefit, where the pension is a fixed percentage of last salary
Defined contribution, where the pension depends on contributions and investment returns
A pay-as-you-go social security scheme
A pure insurance product with guaranteed maturity value
In NPS the contribution is defined and the eventual benefit depends on accumulated corpus and returns.
Retirement Planning: An Overview
For Central Government employees (other than armed forces), the National Pension System replaced the old defined-benefit pension for those joining service on or after:
1 April 2009
1 April 2015
1 January 2004
1 January 1998
NPS became mandatory for new Central Government recruits from 1 January 2004; it opened to all citizens in 2009.
Retirement Planning: An Overview
A client's current monthly expenses are ₹40,000. If inflation averages 6% a year, what will be the equivalent monthly expense in 20 years (approximately)?
₹1.28 lakh
₹1.04 lakh
₹1.53 lakh
Pension Systems & Regulatory Framework (PFRDA)
Under which law does the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) derive its statutory powers?
The PFRDA Act, 2013
The SEBI Act, 1992
The Insurance Act, 1938
The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952
PFRDA was given statutory status by the PFRDA Act, 2013, which governs NPS and its intermediaries.
Pension Systems & Regulatory Framework (PFRDA)
What is the main function of a Central Recordkeeping Agency (CRA) in NPS?
Investing subscriber contributions in equities and bonds
Selling annuities to retiring subscribers
Setting the tax rules for NPS
Maintaining subscriber records, issuing PRANs and providing account administration and grievance handling
The CRA is the record-keeping and administration backbone of NPS; investment is done by pension funds and annuities by insurers.
Pension Systems & Regulatory Framework (PFRDA)
In the NPS architecture, a Point of Presence (POP) is:
The pension fund that manages the money
The entity through which subscribers register and make contributions
The insurer that pays annuities
The trustee that holds legal title to all NPS assets
POPs, such as banks and other registered entities, are the customer-facing access points for NPS subscribers.
Pension Systems & Regulatory Framework (PFRDA)
The Unified Pension Scheme (UPS), introduced from 1 April 2025, is available as an option to:
All self-employed citizens
Private-sector employees covered by EPF
Atal Pension Yojana subscribers
Central Government employees covered under NPS
UPS is an option under NPS for Central Government employees, adding an assured payout element to the contributory structure.
National Pension System – Architecture
What is a PRAN in NPS?
A pension rate notified annually by the government
A unique, portable Permanent Retirement Account Number allotted to each subscriber
A product code for annuity plans
A tax deduction certificate
The PRAN stays with the subscriber across jobs and locations, making NPS portable.
National Pension System – Architecture
Under the all-citizen model, up to what age can an Indian citizen join NPS?
60 years
70 years
65 years
75 years
PFRDA allows citizens aged 18 to 70 to open an NPS account.
National Pension System – Architecture
Which condition must be met to open an NPS Tier II account?
The subscriber must be above 60
The subscriber must be a government employee
The subscriber must close the Tier I account first
The subscriber must hold an active Tier I account
Tier II is an optional add-on account available only to subscribers with an active Tier I account.
National Pension System – Architecture
In the corporate model of NPS, which statement is correct?
Only employers contribute; employees cannot
It is compulsory for every private company
The corpus belongs to the employer until retirement
Employers can enrol employees and contribute to their NPS accounts in addition to employee contributions
Under the corporate model, both employer and employee may contribute, and the accumulated corpus belongs to the employee's PRAN.
National Pension System – Architecture
What happens to an NPS Vatsalya account when the minor attains majority?
It can be converted into a regular NPS account in the subscriber's own name
It is closed and the money is forfeited
It automatically becomes an annuity
It is transferred to the guardian's PRAN
NPS Vatsalya lets guardians save for minors; at 18 the account transitions to a regular NPS account for the young adult.
NPS – Investment Options & Fund Management
In NPS, asset class 'G' invests primarily in:
Central and State Government securities
Equity shares
Corporate bonds
Alternative assets such as REITs and InvITs
NPS asset classes are E (equity), C (corporate debt), G (government securities) and A (alternative investments).
NPS – Investment Options & Fund Management
Under the Auto Choice option in NPS, the allocation to equity:
Reduces progressively as the subscriber ages, according to the chosen life-cycle fund
Remains constant throughout
Increases as the subscriber nears retirement
Is decided monthly by the POP
Life-cycle funds automatically shift from equity to debt with age, de-risking the corpus as retirement nears.
NPS – Investment Options & Fund Management
Under the Active Choice option in NPS, who decides the allocation across asset classes?
The Central Recordkeeping Agency
The NPS Trust for each subscriber individually
The subscriber, within the limits prescribed by PFRDA
The employer in all cases
Active Choice lets the subscriber set the mix among E, C, G and A subject to regulatory caps.
NPS – Investment Options & Fund Management
Priya, 26, has a high risk appetite and wants maximum equity in NPS but prefers the portfolio to de-risk automatically with age. Which option suits her?
Auto Choice – Conservative Life Cycle Fund (LC25)
Active Choice with 100% in asset class G
Tier II account with 100% in asset class C
Auto Choice – Aggressive Life Cycle Fund (LC75)
LC75 offers the highest starting equity among life-cycle funds and tapers it automatically as she ages.
NPS – Exit, Withdrawal & Annuity
Which of the following is NOT a permitted ground for partial withdrawal from an NPS Tier I account?
Buying a car
Higher education of children
